tagline: Country roads link working farms, cypress water and a Seminole battlefield
intro: The Scenic Sumter Heritage Byway runs 62 miles through working farms, ranches, forests and waterways in Sumter County. Open fields give way to hardwood forest, with moss-covered cypress along the Withlacoochee River and Lake Panasoffkee among the route’s water landmarks. Designated a Florida Scenic Highway in 2013, the corridor was created to preserve and share the area’s natural, recreational and historic resources. In 1925, Travelon Magazine called Sumter County the “storehouse of Florida” and described making a good living on ten acres, an agricultural ambition tied to the landscape this corridor now shares.

The campaign brought together the county chamber of commerce, Webster and Bushnell, county government, businesses, veterans’ groups and residents. The route entered the state program as a candidate in 2010; after designation, supporters gathered at Dade Battlefield in January 2014 to cut the ribbon. The battlefield was one of the historic places included along the new byway.

From Rutland, State Road 44 crosses the Withlacoochee, and County Road 470 follows Lake Panasoffkee’s west side toward Sumterville. Bushnell lies south of Sumterville, with Dade Battlefield beside the city. Farther south, St. Catherine stands on U.S. 301; Linden lies on State Road 50, with Webster to its north.

moments.title: Rutland
moments.text: At Rutland, State Road 44 enters Sumter County on a bridge across the Withlacoochee River. The river borders the community to the southwest, while Lake Panasoffkee lies to the southeast. Farming and recreation are the main local industries. County Road 470 continues along the lake’s west side toward Sumterville, linking the river crossing with the lake country farther along the drive.

moments.title: Lake Panasoffkee
moments.text: Black Seminoles settled near Boggy Island at Lake Panasoffkee around 1813, naming their settlement Sitarkey’s Village after an Alachua Seminole who had settled there. They raised corn, rice and sugar cane, along with cattle, horses and hogs. During the Second Seminole War, families used the area as a refuge. After the battle of Wahoo Swamp, Osceola moved to Panasoffkee Swamp to live with Black Seminoles. General Thomas Sidney Jesup raided the village in January 1837, capturing 16 Black Seminoles while others escaped. Seminoles also held councils and Green Corn Dances in the Lake Panasoffkee area.

moments.title: Dade Battlefield
moments.text: A military road ran through the ground now preserved at Dade Battlefield. Soldiers and enslaved people cut the Fort King Road through pines and understory in 1828, making a passage 20 feet wide. On December 28, 1835, Seminole warriors and Black Seminole allies fought Major Francis L. Dade’s soldiers here. The United States was attempting to force the Seminoles from Florida to Indian Territory. The battle began the Second Seminole War. The park preserves pine flatwoods and a live oak hammock; the breastworks near its museum are a replica. The museum explains the Seminole War, while a nature trail winds through the pine flatwoods.
